Binding a prefix to an account is a membership check. npm grants a scope that matches the user or organization name at signup; only members of that scope can publish into it. A one-owner marketplace implements the same rule as UNIQUE(owner_id, local_name) plus a publish ACL. No human is required to enforce the ACL once the scope exists. It does not, by itself, stop someone from registering an unused brand scope first.

Trusted publishing exchanges a short-lived OIDC token from a named IdP (GitHub Actions, GitLab, CircleCI) against a preconfigured trust policy. Verification is cryptographic (JWT signature + claims). PyPI, npm, and the OpenSSF trusted-publishers profile all describe this as an automated publisher-to-CI binding. It does not prove that the package author is a named legal entity. npm does not even verify the saved configuration until publish time.

A blue-check / verified badge that means 'this publisher is the real vendor' is not the OIDC check. VS Code Marketplace requires a Marketplace-team review of legitimacy, trust and positive reputation within 5 business days after DNS TXT succeeds. NuGet prefix applications go to account@nuget.org and 'may need to ask additional identifying questions'. DNS TXT is automatable; the reputation and identity judgment is not. A staffless marketplace cannot honestly issue this badge.

Once a grant exists, PEP 752 requires uploads matching the reserved namespace to fail with HTTP 409 unless the uploader holds the grant. NuGet rejects submissions on a reserved ID prefix unless they come from the prefix owner. That is a string-prefix ACL a single owner can run with no staff. It does not decide who receives the grant.

Issuing the grant is a judgment: PEP 755 approval criteria include whether the namespace 'properly and clearly identify the reservation owner' and whether not reserving it 'may cause ambiguity, confusion, or other harm'. Applications 'require independent review'. PEP 541 name-retention disputes are tickets against pypi/support; the Packaging Workgroup has the final say. crates.io's RFC 3463 lets the team delete crates that exist only to squat a name. A staffless marketplace can seed a static well-known list; it cannot adjudicate competing claims.

Warehouse check_project_name raises ProjectNameUnavailableSimilarError when ultranormalize_name(existing) equals ultranormalize_name(candidate). The SQL function strips separators and maps l/i->1 and o->0. That is a pure function over names plus an index; a staffless marketplace can run it at register time. It is not a general Levenshtein gate: requets vs requests and pydantic2 vs pydantic are documented misses.

The captured warehouse.packaging.tasks.typo_check_project_name runs *after* the create transaction commits. It records ObservationKind.IsTypoSnyperMatch 'for admin review'. The source states this is a record only and nothing about the project's lifecycle changes. Without staff to act on the queue, the check is telemetry, not a defense. A staffless marketplace that copies this pattern has not implemented typo-distance blocking.

Temporal replay re-executes the Workflow Function against Event History and requires it to emit the same sequence of Commands; a mismatch is a non-determinism error. Workflow code must be deterministic to support replay.

Temporal names LLM/AI invocations as non-deterministic operations that must be placed in Activities. Activities run once; the result is recorded in Event History and is reused, not recomputed, on replay. An LLM call inlined in Workflow code would take a network path that is not in history and can diverge on re-execution.

Restate journals Context operations. Non-deterministic operations must be wrapped (ctx.run / ctx.run_typed) so replay stores and reuses the result. The Python SDK schedules the run closure only if the run wasn't replayed. Official docs wrap an LLM call as ctx.run_typed("LLM call", ...).

DBOS requires a workflow function to be deterministic: given the same inputs and the same step return values, it must invoke the same steps with the same inputs in the same order. Third-party API calls must not run directly in the workflow function. Recovery uses check_operation_execution and, if recorded_step_output exists, replays the checkpoint instead of re-entering the step body.

The specific determinism property an LLM step breaks is command-sequence (or journal-entry / step-sequence) identity of the orchestration function under replay. LLM sampling and HTTP I/O are not functions of recorded history; re-executing them inside the replayed function can emit a different command/journal/step sequence. Wrapping the call as an Activity, ctx.run, or @DBOS.step does not make the model deterministic — it moves the non-determinism off the replay path so the recorded bytes can be reused. Replay of an LLM workflow is therefore not 'partially possible': the LLM invocation is excluded from the replayed function, and the remaining orchestration is fully constrained to recorded results.

The subset that CAN be replayed deterministically is: (1) pure control-flow in the orchestration function that branches only on values already recorded in history/journal/checkpoints; (2) SDK-wrapped time, timers, and UUIDs whose results are journaled; (3) versioning/patch markers that select a recorded code path; (4) the scheduling of side-effect wrappers, not their live re-execution. Explicitly excluded: LLM token sampling, raw HTTP, unrecorded wall-clock, unrecorded PRNG, and process-local mutable globals.

How do durable-execution engines achieve deterministic replay (event-sourced history, side-effect wrapping, versioned code paths), and which of those constraints can a workflow whose steps are non-deterministic LLM calls actually satisfy?

Map-over-unknown-N is the Map state (Distributed mode). The barrier is Map Run completion. K-of-N is ToleratedFailureCount / ToleratedFailurePercentage; both default to zero, so any child failure fails the map.

Map-over-unknown-N is a chord header group. The barrier is the chord body, which runs only after every header task has returned. Any header exception fails the callback with ChordError; remaining header tasks still run.

Map-over-unknown-N is mapped task expansion (expand()). The barrier is the downstream task's trigger_rule over mapped indexes. Default all_success requires every upstream mapped index to succeed before the reduce/join runs.

Map-over-unknown-N is withItems/withParam template expansion. The barrier is template/DAG completion. Template failFast fails the template when any child pod has failed. DAG failFast defaults true: stop scheduling new nodes on first failure, then wait for in-flight nodes before failing the DAG.

Map-over-unknown-N is N concurrent activity invocations joined by the workflow. Contrast with the local pathology: an Activity Execution MUST set Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close. Default Schedule-To-Close is infinity, but the docs still require one of the two fields.
Map-over-unknown-N is firing one activity per item without await, then Task.WhenAll as the barrier. WhenAll completes only after every work item completes; a faulted child faults WhenAll.

Map-N is Map/expand/withItems/chord-header/WhenAll/concurrent activities. Barriers are map-run completion, trigger_rule, failFast, chord body, or Task.WhenAll. Default K-of-N is almost always K=N except AWS Distributed Map, which exposes an explicit tolerated-failure budget defaulting to zero. The local no-timeout pathology is named on Celery: task_time_limit defaults to 'No time limit', so a hung chord header never unlocks.

Azure Logic Apps Until is a condition-terminated loop: the workflow runs inner actions, then evaluates an expression; the loop stops when the expression is true. The engine documents default limits that stop the loop to prevent endless loops.
Until-loop iteration default is 60 (min 1, max 5,000) and timeout default is PT1H on multitenant / stateful single-tenant; stateless single-tenant timeout default is PT5M.

n8n Loop Over Items with Reset plus an If node evaluates an exit condition per iteration. The docs warn that if the termination condition never matches, the workflow execution gets stuck in an infinite loop. The infinite-loop guard is optional: an infinite loop is expressible.

LangGraph cyclic graphs stop on a stop-condition edge or when recursion_limit is exhausted. Exhaustion raises GraphRecursionError, documented as preventing infinite loops. The limit is always present (must be >= 1) and is raisable via config.
Airflow sensors are a condition-terminated wait: they poke until a criteria is met and fail when they time out. timeout is a BaseSensorOperator parameter documented on all sensors.
When BaseSensorOperator.timeout is None, Airflow reads sensors.default_timeout from config. The config template default is 604800 seconds (7 days).

Step Functions has no native Until/While. Condition-terminated iteration is expressed by a Choice state (JSONPath/JSONata rules) looping via Next. Standard executions have a hard quota of 25,000 events in a single execution history; reaching it fails the execution. Maximum execution time is 1 year (Standard) or 5 minutes (Express).

Temporal Workflows may loop on arbitrary conditions in code. Continue-As-New resets Event History so a Workflow can run forever. Workflow Execution Timeout exists but Temporal's Python SDK docs generally do not recommend setting Workflow Timeouts. The iteration/stop guard is optional: an infinite loop is expressible.

Durable Task eternal orchestrations are documented as running indefinitely. continue-as-new resets orchestration history so an infinite loop can run without unbounded history growth. That API is a history-management pattern, not a mandatory stop rule. An infinite loop is expressible and first-class.
Every surveyed engine that can express a condition-terminated loop also installs a mandatory finite iteration cap, so an infinite loop is never expressible.

Seven engines were captured with two rails each. Azure Logic Apps Until, LangGraph recursion_limit, Airflow sensors, and AWS Step Functions Choice loops have mandatory finite backstops (iteration/timeout/history quotas). n8n Reset+If, Temporal Continue-As-New, and Durable Functions eternal orchestrations make an infinite loop expressible: their documented guards are optional or are history-reset patterns rather than stop rules. Condition evaluation is engine-specific (Until expression, If node, graph edges, sensor poke, Choice rules, SDK code).

Equal-weight linear pooling is defined from the current member probabilities alone and is therefore usable at zero labelled history.
